Loan and Mortgage Jargon, Translated

APR, APRC, LTV, LTI, ERC, SVC, roll-up, balloon, 58-day rule. Both vocabularies in one place, in plain English.

Loans and mortgages use two vocabularies that overlap, and the overlap is usually where the confusion lives — APR and APRC aren't the same measure, and "variable rate" means something different depending on which product you're holding. Here are both sets, explained in one place.

Rates and how cost is measured

APR — Annual Percentage Rate. This adds interest and any compulsory fees together and expresses them as a yearly rate, for consumer credit. It's designed for comparing two agreements of the same amount and term. Because it can't see term length, it won't tell you that a seven-year loan costs far more than a three-year one at the same APR.

Representative APR — the rate offered to at least 51% of accepted applicants. That leaves up to 49% who can lawfully be paying more. It's not a personal quote.

APRC — Annual Percentage Rate of Charge, the mortgage equivalent of APR. It includes fees and assumes you keep the mortgage for its full term, which almost nobody does, so it's a poor way to choose between fixed deals. Compare the total cost over the fixed period instead.

Total amount payable / total cost of credit — everything you'll hand over by the end. It's the one figure that can't be flattered by stretching the term, which is why it's the one worth comparing. See why.

Base rate — the Bank of England's rate. Trackers follow it directly; standard variable rates are influenced by it but set by the lender.

SVR — Standard Variable Rate. Your lender's default rate, where you land once a deal ends. It's typically well above what you could arrange elsewhere, and drifting onto it is one of the most common avoidable mortgage costs.

Tracker — a rate that follows base rate by a fixed margin. It moves transparently.

Discount rate — a reduction from the lender's own SVR. Because the lender sets the SVR themselves, they can move your rate without base rate moving at all.

Fixed rate — a rate that can't change for a set period. You're paying for certainty here, not necessarily for a cheaper deal. See choosing between them.

Mortgage-specific

LTV — Loan to Value. Your borrowing, as a percentage of the property's value. It's priced in bands, and crossing a band boundary changes the rate on the whole mortgage, which is why a small extra deposit is sometimes worth a great deal, and sometimes worth almost nothing.

LTI — Loan to Income. Your borrowing, as a multiple of income. Lenders are limited in how much of their new lending they can write above 4.5x, which is why offers tend to cluster just below it.

ERC — Early Repayment Charge. What it costs you to leave a deal early, commonly 1–5% of the balance, tapering as the years pass. It's the part of a long fix that turns it into a genuine commitment.

Product fee — the arrangement fee for a specific mortgage deal. Add it to the loan and you'll pay interest on it for the whole term.

Porting — moving your existing mortgage deal across to a new property, keeping the rate and avoiding the ERC. It isn't automatic; you have to qualify again.

Product transfer — a new deal from your existing lender without a full remortgage. Quicker, with less paperwork, but you're choosing from just one lender's range.

Repayment vs interest-only — a repayment mortgage clears capital and interest together, so the debt ends. Interest-only pays the interest alone, so the full balance is still owed at the end and you need a credible plan to repay it.

Amortisation — how a repayment balance actually reduces over time. Early payments are mostly interest; capital repayment speeds up later on. You can see it in the repayment calculator.

Negative equity — when the mortgage exceeds the property's value. Both remortgaging and moving become very difficult.

Decision in principle / AIP — an indication, not a mortgage. The lender still looks again before completion, and can change their mind.

Second charge — a loan secured on your property, behind the main mortgage. It's regulated as a mortgage, and priced higher than a first charge but lower than unsecured borrowing.

SDLT — Stamp Duty Land Tax, payable on completion, with a surcharge on additional properties. Rates change, so use the calculator and check gov.uk.

Equity release / lifetime mortgage — borrowing against your home in later life, with the interest usually rolled up rather than paid monthly. Compounding runs against you here; see the cost calculator.

Bridging loan — short-term borrowing priced monthly, to cover a gap. Fast, and expensive.

Loan and credit-specific

Secured vs unsecured — whether the debt's attached to an asset. This decides the rate, and it decides what happens if you can't pay. See what changes.

Early settlement / the 58-day rule — you have a statutory right to settle a regulated agreement early. The lender can add up to 28 days' interest, and up to 30 more on agreements over twelve months. Hence "58 days".

PCP — Personal Contract Purchase. You pay the depreciation monthly and face an optional final balloon payment. Lower monthly cost, higher total cost, and you own nothing unless you also pay the balloon.

HP — Hire Purchase. You pay the whole cost over the term and own the car at the end. Higher monthly cost, lower total cost.

GFV — Guaranteed Future Value. The balloon figure on a PCP, set at the outset.

Voluntary termination — once you've paid 50% of the total amount payable on a regulated HP or PCP, you may hand the car back and owe nothing further. It's a statutory right, and it isn't the same thing as voluntary surrender, where the debt remains.

Fair wear and tear — the BVRLA standard used to assess a returned vehicle. It's published and specific, so it's worth checking your car against it before an inspector does.

Section 75 — Consumer Credit Act protection that makes the card provider jointly liable with the retailer, for purchases between £100 and £30,000. Credit cards only, not debit cards.

Right to withdraw — you get 14 days to withdraw from most regulated credit agreements after signing. You repay what you borrowed plus any interest that's built up.

Hard vs soft search — a hard search is recorded on your file and visible to other lenders; a soft search isn't. Eligibility checkers are soft.

Utilisation — how much of your available credit you're using. Lower is better, and it updates monthly.

Default — a formal record that an agreement broke down. It stays on your file for six years from the date it's recorded.

CCJ — County Court Judgment. Six years on your file. If it's left unpaid, it can lead to a charging order, which secures a previously unsecured debt against your home.

Breathing Space — the Debt Respite Scheme. Up to 60 days with interest, fees and enforcement paused while you get advice. You apply for it through a debt adviser.

DMP — Debt Management Plan. An informal arrangement to pay non-priority creditors at a reduced rate, usually set up through a free charity.

IVA — Individual Voluntary Arrangement. A formal, binding insolvency arrangement. It has serious consequences and isn't right for everyone, so take free advice before you consider one.

Anything here you'd explain differently, or a term we've missed? These pages get revised, and the vocabulary is the part most worth getting right.
